title: Media studies futures: Whiteness, indigeneity, multi-modality, and a politics of possibility
apa: Henderson, L. (2020). Media studies futures: Whiteness, indigeneity, multi-modality, and a politics of possibility. *Television & New Media, 21*(6), 581-589. https://doi.org/10.1177/1527476420921515
summary: Henderson, writing as a media studies dean, reflects on where the field should go next. Using Hannah Gadsby's stand-up special Nanette as a touchstone, she argues that the discipline needs to divest from its default whiteness, take Indigenous knowledge and multi-modal scholarship seriously, and cultivate a politics of possibility rather than only critique.
analysis: The essay is a programmatic intervention rather than an empirical study, and its evidence is institutional experience, the #CommunicationSoWhite critique of citation and hiring patterns, and a close reading of a comedic performance. Its main contribution is to treat the field's future as a question of who produces knowledge and in what forms, not only what topics it studies. By pairing divestment from whiteness with investment in Indigenous and multi-modal work, it links representation inside the academy to the representational critiques media studies aims at industry. A limit is that the prescription stays at the level of disposition and institutional will, with few concrete mechanisms for redistributing resources or authority, and it is written largely from a Canadian and Anglo-American vantage. It sets up the course's recurring lens on centering whiteness and the West, which returns in Hall's white eye, Steele, Brock, and Couldry and Mejias.
note: Her notes list this as Communication and Critical/Cultural Studies 17(1); Crossref shows the article titled Media Studies Futures is in Television & New Media 21(6), 2020. Confirm against the syllabus PDF.

title: Situation critical
apa: Hearn, A. (2013). Situation critical. *Communication and Critical/Cultural Studies, 10*(2-3), 273-279. https://doi.org/10.1080/14791420.2013.814414
summary: Part of a keywords forum in which scholars reflected on the three terms in the journal's title, Hearn asks what being critical can still mean when critique itself has become a marketable posture. She argues for critique grounded in a clear reading of the present conjuncture of capitalism, labor, and self-branding, rather than critique as a signature style.
analysis: Hearn works through immanent critique: she tests the field's claims to criticality against the political economic conditions in which academics and media workers now labor. Her contribution is to connect the academic word critical to her broader research on promotional culture and the branded self, showing that the university and the platform economy share a logic of self-promotion. The short forum format makes the piece suggestive rather than systematic, and its examples come mostly from North American and British contexts. It pairs with Henderson as a first-week framing of what the course means by critical, and it previews the chapter 6 split between political economy and cultural studies, as well as Banet-Weiser on branded authenticity and Smythe on audience labor.

title: Understanding and evaluating mass communication theory
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Understanding and evaluating mass communication theory. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The opening chapter defines theory and explains why mass communication has several kinds of it rather than one. It introduces the ontological, epistemological, and axiological commitments that separate postpositivist, hermeneutic, critical, and normative theory, and it previews the historical trends the book will trace.
analysis: The chapter's central move is to treat theory as a set of competing ways of knowing, each with its own standards of evidence and its own stance on values. Its framework for evaluating theory gives students a vocabulary they will reuse all term when weighing strengths and weaknesses in the Instant Access boxes. A strength is its insistence that no single paradigm owns the field, which legitimizes the critical and cultural work assigned later. A limit is that the paradigm story is told from a largely United States disciplinary history, so non-Western theory appears mostly as context rather than as a source of theory. Read with Henderson and Hearn, it raises the question of whether the textbook's taxonomy itself reproduces the whiteness those essays critique.

title: Establishing the terms of the debate over media: The first trend in mass communication theory: Mass society and propaganda theories
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Establishing the terms of the debate over media: The first trend in mass communication theory: Mass society and propaganda theories. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter traces mass society theory from late nineteenth century elite anxieties about industrialization and the penny press, and then turns to interwar propaganda theory. It closes by showing how both traditions return in current debates about populism, disinformation, and platform manipulation.
analysis: Baran and Davis reconstruct mass society theory as six assumptions, from powerful direct media effects to the debasement of high culture, and ground it in Tonnies and Durkheim. The propaganda section links behaviorism and Freudian psychology to Lasswell's master symbols, Lippmann's pseudo-environment, and Dewey's democratic reply. The chapter's contribution is to show that the first trend set the terms of later debate, even where later scholars rejected its conclusions. A limit, noted by historians such as Sproule and Pooley, is that the tidy magic bullet story is partly a straw man built by the later effects school, and the chapter only partly corrects that myth. It pairs directly with Lippmann and sets up the normative theories in chapter 3.

title: The world outside and the pictures in our heads
apa: Lippmann, W. (1922). The world outside and the pictures in our heads. In *Public opinion* (pp. 3-32). Harcourt, Brace.
summary: The first chapter of Public Opinion opens with islanders who lived as friends for weeks after their nations went to war because the news had not arrived. Lippmann argues that everyone acts on a mental picture of the world that sits between them and reality, and that this pseudo-environment, not the world itself, drives behavior.
analysis: Lippmann builds his case through vivid historical anecdotes rather than systematic data: wartime hero worship, medieval maps, and staged military photographs. His key contribution is the pseudo-environment, a concept that makes mediated representation the central problem of democratic life and anticipates agenda setting and framing. He treats fictions as necessary simplifications, not lies, and locates the difficulty in the scale and complexity of modern society rather than in popular stupidity. The strongest critique is that his later technocratic remedy, an expert bureau filtering information, sidelines public deliberation, which is exactly what Dewey attacked. Read against chapter 2, the primary text is more careful than the textbook's bewildered herd summary, and it anticipates algorithmic feeds as machine-built pictures in our heads.
note: Public domain. Page range is for the Harcourt, Brace first edition chapter 1; ISBN is the Free Press paperback. Her notes also cite the New Republic serialization (1922, vol. 30, pp. 10-14).

title: Normative theories of mass communication
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Normative theories of mass communication. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter surveys prescriptive theories about how media ought to operate, from authoritarian and libertarian models through social responsibility theory and the Hutchins Commission. It extends the discussion to the role of journalism ethics, objectivity, and the regulation of online platforms.
analysis: Normative theory is judged here by its ideals rather than by empirical prediction, and the chapter traces how libertarian faith in a self-righting marketplace of ideas gave way to social responsibility after the 1947 Hutchins report. Its contribution is to show that media policy debates, from the Fairness Doctrine to Section 230, are arguments among these normative models. The chapter usefully flags the benevolent technocracy at the heart of social responsibility, where experts decide what the public needs. A limit is its heavy focus on the United States First Amendment tradition, with other national and non-Western press systems treated mainly as foils. It pairs with Adams-Bloom and Cleary, who try to reconcile profit and public service, and with Couldry and Mejias later on platform governance.

title: Staking a claim for social responsibility: An argument for the dual responsibility model
apa: Adams-Bloom, T., & Cleary, J. (2009). Staking a claim for social responsibility: An argument for the dual responsibility model. *International Journal on Media Management, 11*(1), 1-8. https://doi.org/10.1080/14241270802518356
summary: The authors argue that news organizations should be understood as having two obligations at once, to shareholders and to the public. They propose a dual responsibility model that borrows from stakeholder theory to show how media firms can remain profitable while meeting social responsibility norms.
analysis: This is a conceptual essay that updates social responsibility theory for an era of publicly traded, consolidated media companies. Its contribution is to move the normative debate out of journalism ethics and into management theory, treating public service as a stakeholder claim a firm must balance. The argument is brief and largely untested, and it assumes that market pressure and civic duty can be reconciled through managerial will. Critics in the political economy tradition would reply that the ownership structures described by Smythe and chapter 6 make that balance structurally unstable. The model also anticipates later debates over whether profit-driven platforms can be asked to serve the public, taken up by Couldry and Mejias and by Roberts.

title: The emergence of the media-effects trend in mass communication theory
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). The emergence of the media-effects trend in mass communication theory. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: This chapter follows the turn from speculative mass society theory to empirical research in the 1940s, led by Lazarsfeld's survey work and Hovland's persuasion experiments. It explains how findings of limited, conditional effects produced a new paradigm.
analysis: The chapter's argument is that method changed theory: once researchers used panel surveys and controlled experiments, they found that media usually reinforced existing attitudes rather than converting people. It introduces the People's Choice study, the two-step flow, selective processes, and the Yale persuasion variables. A strength is its clear account of how postpositivist standards became the field's default. A limit, which later critics such as Gitlin pressed, is that the limited effects label served media industries and funders and narrowed attention to short-term individual attitude change. It frames Hovland, Janis, and Kelley directly and sets up chapter 6's critical reaction.

title: Communication and persuasion: Psychological studies of opinion change
apa: Hovland, C. I., Janis, I. L., & Kelley, H. H. (1953). *Communication and persuasion: Psychological studies of opinion change*. Yale University Press.
summary: The Yale Communication Research Program's summary volume reports a series of experiments on what makes persuasive messages work. It examines the credibility of the communicator, fear appeals, message organization, group membership, individual differences in persuasibility, and how long attitude change lasts.
analysis: The book models the controlled variation approach: isolate one feature of a message or source, manipulate it, and measure attitude change in student or military samples. Its lasting contributions include source credibility research and the sleeper effect, the finding that a low-credibility message can gain influence over time as its source is forgotten. It made persuasion a program of cumulative, testable variables and trained a generation of effects researchers. The major limit is external validity: short laboratory exposures with mostly white, male, American participants say little about long-term cultural influence or audiences outside that frame. Chapter 4 presents it as a founding effects text, and chapter 6 and Hall later show what this variable-based approach could not see.
note: read_url is an Internet Archive controlled digital lending copy (free borrow with account). No ISBN on the 1953 edition.

title: The consolidation of the media effects trend
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). The consolidation of the media effects trend. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter shows how limited effects findings hardened into a dominant perspective through Klapper's phenomenistic approach, functionalism, and information flow and diffusion research. It explains why the effects trend dominated American communication research through the 1960s.
analysis: Baran and Davis argue that the effects trend consolidated because it fit the era's institutional funding, its faith in science, and its pluralist view of democracy. Klapper's synthesis, the two-step flow, and diffusion of innovations are presented as its high points, along with functional analysis of what media do for society. The chapter credits the trend with rigor and cumulative findings. It also notes the cost: a focus on short-term individual effects and an assumption that the social order was basically sound. It frames Katz and Lazarsfeld and anticipates the critical cultural backlash in chapter 6.

title: Personal influence: The part played by people in the flow of mass communications
apa: Katz, E., & Lazarsfeld, P. F. (1955). *Personal influence: The part played by people in the flow of mass communications*. Free Press.
summary: Based on interviews with about 800 women in Decatur, Illinois, the book examines how opinions about marketing, fashion, public affairs, and movies spread through everyday conversation. It develops the two-step flow model, in which opinion leaders attend to media and pass ideas on to others through personal networks.
analysis: The Decatur study used survey interviews and follow-ups to trace influence episodes, and it found that opinion leaders were spread across social strata rather than concentrated at the top. Its central contribution is to rediscover the primary group, showing that interpersonal relationships mediate media influence. The introduction also helped invent the story that earlier research assumed atomized audiences, a narrative later historians such as Pooley call an origin myth. Critics such as Gitlin note that the study was funded by a publisher interested in reaching consumers, that much opinion change involved no remembered personal contact, and that its focus on women as consumers reflects the gendered assumptions of 1950s market research. It extends chapter 5 and returns in platform research on influencers and networked two-step flow.
note: read_url is an Internet Archive controlled digital lending copy of the 1964 printing. ISBN is the current Routledge/Transaction paperback.

title: The political economy of heteronormativity
apa: Nguyen, D. H. (2023). The political economy of heteronormativity. *Review of Radical Political Economics, 55*(1), 112-131. https://doi.org/10.1177/04866134211011269
summary: Nguyen revisits the Fraser and Butler debate over whether queer oppression is economic or cultural, reading it through social reproduction theory. The article argues that heteronormativity helps capitalism reproduce itself and that neoliberalism now divides queer people with capital from those without.
analysis: The method is theoretical synthesis, drawing on Marxist feminist social reproduction theory to reframe a debate usually staged as recognition versus redistribution. Its contribution is to show that heteronormative family forms perform material work for capital, which means queer liberation requires political economic change, not only visibility. It also critiques mainstream LGBT progress narratives for masking class stratification among queer people. A limit is that the argument stays at the level of theory with little empirical case material, and its account of neoliberalism is largely drawn from North American and European contexts. It links the political economy tradition in chapter 6 and Smythe to later readings on visibility and representation, including Cavalcante, Warner, and Banet-Weiser.
note: Classmate's article presentation on Sep 28. Online-first 2021, print issue 2023.

title: The emergence of the critical cultural trend in North America
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). The emergence of the critical cultural trend in North America. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter explains how critical and cultural theories rose in the 1960s and 1970s as the effects paradigm lost explanatory power. It traces Marxism, the Frankfurt School, British cultural studies, political economy, Carey's ritual view, news production research, critical feminist scholarship, and McLuhan.
analysis: Baran and Davis frame the trend as a shift from measuring effects to interpreting how media shape culture, identity, and power over the long term. The chapter's key distinctions are micro cultural studies versus macro political economy, structuralist versus culturalist Marxism, and transmission versus ritual models of communication. It credits the trend with asking big questions about control and ownership while noting its lack of scientific verification. A limit is that critical theory is narrated largely as a European import to North America, so scholars of color and anti-colonial thinkers appear late, mostly under intersectionality. It is the theoretical frame for Hall's essay, for Smythe on Oct 5, and for most readings in the second half of the course.

title: The whites of their eyes: Racist ideologies and the media
apa: Hall, S. (2021). The whites of their eyes: Racist ideologies and the media. In C. Brunsdon (Ed.), *Writings on media: History of the present* (pp. 177-200). Duke University Press. (Original work published 1981)
summary: Hall asks how British media construct the meaning of race so as to reproduce racist ideology, often without anyone intending it, and how the left can intervene. He distinguishes overt racism from inferential racism, traces a colonial grammar of race in television genres, and defends a popular strategy for anti-racist media work.
analysis: The essay combines a theory of ideology as chains of meaning with close readings of British adventure films, sitcoms, and news coverage such as the 1979 Southall protests. Its central contribution is inferential racism: racist premises built into apparently neutral or liberal representations that are invisible even to those who produce them, so bias does not require intent. Hall rejects both conspiracy models of media and economic determinism, treating media as a plural but unequal site of struggle, which is the culturalist position chapter 6 names. A limit is that the analysis is rooted in 1970s British television and does not systematically examine audiences, so claims about how viewers take up these images remain inferred. It anticipates Brock, Steele, and later work on algorithmic classification, where bias lives in system premises rather than individual intent.
note: Verified: chapter 14 of the Duke University Press volume in the Stuart Hall: Selected Writings series (Brunsdon, Ed., 2021). Originally in G. Bridges & R. Brunt (Eds.), Silver linings: Some strategies for the eighties (pp. 28-52), Lawrence and Wishart. It is not in the Essential Essays volumes.

title: Communications: Blindspot of Western Marxism
apa: Smythe, D. W. (1977). Communications: Blindspot of Western Marxism. *Canadian Journal of Political and Social Theory, 1*(3), 1-27.
summary: Smythe argues that Western Marxists misread mass media by treating them mainly as producers of ideology. He proposes that the main commodity of advertiser-supported media is the audience itself, whose attention is sold to advertisers, so audiences perform unpaid work for capital.
analysis: This is a polemical theoretical essay that reframes media economics through Marx's labor theory of value. Its contribution, the audience commodity thesis, made advertising and audience measurement central to political economy and set off the blindspot debate with Murdock and others. The thesis now reads as prophetic for platforms that monetize user attention and data. Critics argue that watching is not labor in any strict sense, that the model neglects how audiences interpret content, and that it generalizes from North American commercial broadcasting to media everywhere. It is the political economy counterpart to Hall in chapter 6, and it leads directly to Couldry and Mejias on data colonialism and Roberts on platform labor.
note: Syllabus lists only Smythe on this date with no chapter; chose his best-known political economy essay, which follows chapter 6's political economy section. Free from the University of Victoria journal archive.

title: Theories of media and social learning
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Theories of media and social learning. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter covers theories that explain how people learn behavior from media, with a focus on the long debate over television violence. It moves from early violence research to Bandura's social learning and social cognitive theory, and then to the general aggression model and newer media.
analysis: The chapter's argument is that social learning theory gave effects research a sturdier model than simple imitation by adding attention, retention, motivation, and self-efficacy. It reviews the Surgeon General reports and experimental and longitudinal evidence on aggression, noting why industry and researchers disagreed over the size of effects. A strength is its demonstration that effects research did not end with limited effects but moved toward conditional, cumulative claims. A limit is that the research base relies heavily on lab studies of American children, and the chapter pays less attention to how race, class, and gender shape which models are shown and imitated. It frames Bandura and connects forward to cultivation in chapter 12.

title: Social cognitive theory of mass communication
apa: Bandura, A. (2001). Social cognitive theory of mass communication. *Media Psychology, 3*(3), 265-299. https://doi.org/10.1207/S1532785XMEP0303_03
summary: Bandura lays out how symbolic modeling in media shapes thought, emotion, and behavior through attention, retention, production, and motivation. He adds a dual path account in which media influence people both directly and through the social networks that adopt what media model, illustrated with entertainment education campaigns.
analysis: The article is a theoretical synthesis of decades of experimental work, framed by triadic reciprocal causation among person, behavior, and environment. Its contribution is to position audiences as agents with self-regulatory capacities while still explaining powerful cumulative media influence. The entertainment education examples, including serial dramas in Mexico, India, and Tanzania, show how the theory was applied to health and social change. A critique is that those campaigns often exported Western development priorities, and the model treats culture as a set of behaviors to be shaped rather than as meanings audiences negotiate. It connects to chapter 7, to the two-step flow through its social pathway, and contrasts with Hall and Gray's more interpretive audiences.
note: Syllabus lists only Bandura; chose his 2001 statement specifically about mass communication, which pairs with chapter 7.

title: Theories of media and human development
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Theories of media and human development. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter examines how media shape development across the life course, especially childhood and adolescence. It covers active theories of children's television viewing, the idea of media as a super peer, body image and sexualization research, and the developmental effects of digital media.
analysis: Baran and Davis organize the chapter around the claim that media are a primary agent of socialization, competing with family, school, and peers. The chapter weighs active and reactive models of young audiences and reviews the evidence on media and body image, gender roles, and sexual attitudes. It is strong in showing how developmental psychology fed communication theory. A limit is that much of the reviewed research assumes a white, middle-class Western child as the norm and measures harm more readily than agency or pleasure. It frames Fredrickson et al. and objectification theory and anticipates the postfeminism debates on Nov 4.

title: That swimsuit becomes you: Sex differences in self-objectification, restrained eating, and math performance
apa: Fredrickson, B. L., Roberts, T.-A., Noll, S. M., Quinn, D. M., & Twenge, J. M. (1998). That swimsuit becomes you: Sex differences in self-objectification, restrained eating, and math performance. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75*(1), 269-284. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.75.1.269
summary: In two experiments, participants tried on either a swimsuit or a sweater alone in a dressing room and then completed tasks. Women in swimsuits reported more body shame, ate less, and did worse on a math test, while men showed little effect, supporting the idea that a self-objectifying state costs women emotionally and cognitively.
analysis: The study operationalizes objectification theory, proposed by Fredrickson and Roberts in 1997, which holds that cultures that sexually objectify women teach them to monitor their bodies from an observer's view. Its contribution is experimental evidence that a brief state of self-objectification has measurable consequences for eating and cognitive performance. The design is clever but relies on white American undergraduates in a contrived setting, so its generalization across race, class, sexuality, and culture is limited, and it does not directly test media exposure. Its concept of an internalized observer echoes Mulvey's male gaze and Hall's white eye from chapter 6. It anchors chapter 8's body image section and sets up Banet-Weiser and Dosekun on how postfeminist culture reworks self-surveillance as empowerment.
note: Syllabus lists Fredrickson et al. The et al. points to the five-author 1998 experiment rather than Fredrickson and Roberts (1997), Objectification theory, Psychology of Women Quarterly, 21(2), 173-206, which is the theory statement. Check the syllabus PDF.

title: Audience theories: Uses and reception
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Audience theories: Uses and reception. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter presents theories that treat audiences as active: uses and gratifications, reception studies, and Hall's encoding and decoding model. It also covers fandom, entertainment theory, and how these approaches apply to interactive and social media.
analysis: The chapter's argument is that shifting the question from what media do to people to what people do with media transformed the field. Uses and gratifications brought a functional, survey-based account of needs, while reception studies, following Hall and Morley, brought an interpretive account of dominant, negotiated, and oppositional readings. A strength is its bridge between postpositivist and cultural traditions. A limit is that the celebration of active audiences can obscure the structural power political economists stress, a tension the chapter itself raises. It frames Gray's work on fans and anti-fans and links back to Hall and forward to Cavalcante's audience study.

title: New audiences, new textualities: Anti-fans and non-fans
apa: Gray, J. (2003). New audiences, new textualities: Anti-fans and non-fans. *International Journal of Cultural Studies, 6*(1), 64-81. https://doi.org/10.1177/1367877903006001004
summary: Gray argues that audience research has focused too narrowly on fans and has ignored anti-fans, who dislike a text intensely, and non-fans, who watch casually. He shows that each group relates to texts at a different distance and therefore encounters a different text.
analysis: The article is a conceptual intervention in fan and reception studies, supported by examples from online discussion and television viewing. Its main contribution is to show that the text is not a stable object: fans, anti-fans, and non-fans build different versions of it from paratexts, hype, and partial viewing. This extends Hall's encoding and decoding and chapter 9's active audience beyond enthusiasts. A limit is that the evidence is illustrative rather than systematic, and the examples come mainly from Anglo-American commercial television. It connects to Cavalcante's transgender audiences, Warner's publics formed through attention, and Brock's Black Twitter, where dislike and critique are also forms of engagement.
note: Syllabus lists only Gray alongside chapter 9 (audience theories). Chose Jonathan Gray's anti-fans article as the best audience-studies fit. Alternatives: Herman Gray, Watching race (1995), or Jonathan Gray, Show sold separately (2010). No class meets Oct 14, but the reading is assigned.

title: Publics and counterpublics
apa: Warner, M. (2002). Publics and counterpublics. *Public Culture, 14*(1), 49-90. https://doi.org/10.1215/08992363-14-1-49
summary: Warner theorizes a public as a relation among strangers created by the circulation of texts, rather than a preexisting group. Counterpublics are publics that know themselves to be subordinate and that circulate discourse whose style and address break with dominant norms, with queer publics as a central example.
analysis: The essay works through a set of propositions about publics, drawing on Habermas while criticizing his rational-critical ideal. Its contribution is to make publics a product of attention and circulation, so that simply paying attention can constitute membership. By defining counterpublics through their manner of address, not just their content, Warner explains why queer and other marginalized discourse is often dismissed as not properly public. A limit is its reliance on print-era circulation and United States queer culture; later scholars ask how race and platform algorithms change who can form and sustain a public. It pairs with Cavalcante, and it is the backbone for Steele's Black digital publics and Brock's Black Twitter.
note: Syllabus lists only Warner; chose the Public Culture article, which is also the lead chapter of the 2002 book of the same name.

title: Breaking into transgender life: Transgender audiences' experiences with "first of its kind" visibility in popular media
apa: Cavalcante, A. (2017). Breaking into transgender life: Transgender audiences' experiences with "first of its kind" visibility in popular media. *Communication, Culture & Critique, 10*(3), 538-555. https://doi.org/10.1111/cccr.12165
summary: Drawing on interviews with transgender people, Cavalcante examines how breakout media texts, the first mainstream portrayals of trans lives, figured in audiences' early understanding of themselves. He shows that such texts could open possibilities for identity even when the portrayals were limited or stigmatizing.
analysis: The study uses qualitative audience interviews, bringing reception studies to a group rarely centered in it. Its contribution is the concept of breakout texts, which captures how first-of-its-kind visibility matters for recognition regardless of a portrayal's quality. It complicates simple positive versus negative image critique by showing that audiences extract resources from flawed representations. A limit is that the sample and texts are mostly American, and the visibility it studies is largely white and mainstream, which leaves open how trans audiences of color read the same texts. It extends Gray and chapter 9 on audiences, pairs with Warner on counterpublics, and connects to Nguyen's warning that visibility can mask economic inequality.
note: Syllabus lists only Cavalcante. Chose his audience-focused article; strong alternatives are I did it all online (2016), Critical Studies in Media Communication, 33(1), 109-122, which pairs with Warner on online publics, or the book Struggling for ordinary (NYU Press, 2018).

title: Effect of media on knowledge, information, and perception of social issues
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Effect of media on knowledge, information, and perception of social issues. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter covers theories of how media shape what people know and think about public issues. It reviews the knowledge gap hypothesis, agenda setting and priming, framing, the spiral of silence, and research on news, misinformation, and polarization.
analysis: Baran and Davis argue that these theories revived powerful effects claims by shifting from attitude change to cognition and salience. Agenda setting and framing are presented as the most productive, with evidence that media influence what issues seem important and how problems are defined. The knowledge gap and spiral of silence show how media effects can deepen inequality and silence minority views. A limit is that most evidence comes from United States news environments and treats publics as national, which fits poorly with networked and diasporic publics. It pairs with Steele on how Black digital publics produce their own knowledge and frames outside the mainstream agenda.

title: Digital Black feminism
apa: Steele, C. K. (2021). *Digital Black feminism*. New York University Press. https://doi.org/10.18574/nyu/9781479808373.001.0001
summary: Steele traces how Black women have used technology, from earlier communication forms to blogs and social media, to build community, share knowledge, and critique power. She argues that Black feminist thought has long shaped digital culture and that Black women's online practices are a form of technical and intellectual labor.
analysis: The book combines historical analysis with close reading of Black women's blogs and social media, and it grounds digital culture in the Black feminist tradition rather than in Silicon Valley histories. Its contribution is to reposition Black women as theorists and innovators of technology, not only as users or targets of harm. It also documents the costs of that labor, including harassment and uncredited appropriation. A limit is that its focus on the United States leaves transnational Black feminist digital practice for others, and the platform economy's ownership structures get less attention than community practices. It connects to Warner's counterpublics, Brock's Black Twitter, Hall's critique of representation, and Roberts on hidden digital labor.
note: Syllabus lists only Steele; likely a chapter of Digital Black Feminism (2021). A strong alternative is Steele (2018), Black bloggers and their varied publics, Television & New Media, 19(2), 112-127, https://doi.org/10.1177/1527476417709535, which follows Warner directly. Check which chapter or article is assigned.

title: Effect of media on community and everyday culture
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Effect of media on community and everyday culture. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter examines macro theories about how media shape shared culture and community life. It centers on cultivation analysis, media literacy, and debates about social capital and community in a networked, platform-based environment.
analysis: The chapter's argument is that some of the most important media effects are slow, cumulative, and shared, visible only at the level of culture. Cultivation is presented as the leading example, with its claims about mainstreaming and resonance, and the chapter weighs the method disputes about measuring viewing and perceptions. It also covers media literacy as a practical response to cultural influence. A limit is that cultivation assumes a relatively centralized television system, which strains in fragmented, algorithmic media markets. It frames Gerbner and Gross and reconnects to mass society concerns about isolation and community from chapter 2.

title: Living with television: The violence profile
apa: Gerbner, G., & Gross, L. (1976). Living with television: The violence profile. *Journal of Communication, 26*(2), 172-199. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1460-2466.1976.tb01397.x
summary: Gerbner and Gross introduce cultivation analysis, arguing that television functions as a common storyteller that cultivates shared assumptions about social reality. Using content analysis of prime-time programs and surveys, they report that heavy viewers are more likely than light viewers to overestimate violence and to see the world as dangerous.
analysis: The Cultural Indicators project combined message system analysis, which counted violence and victimization on television, with cultivation surveys comparing heavy and light viewers. Its contribution was to redefine effects as long-term, shared, and cultural, and to link television violence to social control through fear and the acceptance of authority. The content data also showed that women, older people, and people of color were more often depicted as victims, tying representation to power. Critics such as Hirsch and Newcomb challenged the small correlations, the treatment of viewing as undifferentiated, and inadequate controls for third variables. It extends chapter 12, contrasts with Bandura's individual learning model, and anticipates questions about algorithmic feeds as the new common storyteller.
note: Syllabus lists only Gerbner; chose the foundational 1976 cultivation article that chapter 12 builds on.

title: Media and culture theories: Meaning making in the social world
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Media and culture theories: Meaning making in the social world. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The chapter presents theories that treat communication as the process through which people construct social reality. It covers symbolic interactionism, social construction of reality, framing as a cultural process, and media ritual and collective memory.
analysis: Baran and Davis argue that these perspectives shift attention from transmission of information to the shared meanings that make everyday life intelligible. Symbolic interaction and social constructionism explain how identities and institutions are sustained through talk and media, and framing theory is recast as cultural meaning making rather than only a cognitive effect. A strength is the chapter's bridge from Carey's ritual view to contemporary online interaction. A limit is that meaning making is often described in universal terms, with less attention to how race, gender, and power decide whose meanings stick. It pairs with Brock's analysis of how Black Twitter creates and contests meaning.

title: From the blackhand side: Twitter as a cultural conversation
apa: Brock, A. (2012). From the blackhand side: Twitter as a cultural conversation. *Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media, 56*(4), 529-549. https://doi.org/10.1080/08838151.2012.732147
summary: Brock examines why Black Americans became highly visible on Twitter and how mainstream commentators interpreted that visibility. He argues that Twitter's design fit Black oral and signifying traditions, and that press coverage often read Black Twitter through stereotype rather than as cultural conversation.
analysis: Brock develops critical technocultural discourse analysis, which reads the platform's interface and affordances alongside users' practices and public discourse about them. His contribution is to treat Black Twitter as cultural production shaped by both technology and Black discursive traditions, not as a demographic curiosity. The article also shows mainstream media reproducing the inferential racism Hall described, framing Black participation as spectacle or deficit. A limit is its reliance on public discourse and platform features from one early moment, before algorithmic timelines and the platform's later ownership changes. It connects to chapter 13 on meaning making, Warner's counterpublics, Steele's digital Black feminism, and Hall.
note: Syllabus lists only Brock; chose the 2012 Black Twitter article over Distributed Blackness (2020) because a journal article fits a single class day. The book is the alternative if a chapter is assigned.

title: Media and culture theories: Commodification of culture and mediatization
apa: Baran, S. J., & Davis, D. K. (2021). Media and culture theories: Commodification of culture and mediatization. In *Mass communication theory: Foundations, ferment, and future* (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
summary: The final chapter covers theories about how culture becomes a commodity and how media logics reshape other institutions. It moves from the culture industries and advertising critique to mediatization theory, platform capitalism, and surveillance.
analysis: The chapter argues that commodification and mediatization together describe a world where culture is produced for markets and where institutions from politics to religion adapt to media logics. It revisits the Frankfurt School and political economy while adding newer accounts of branding, platforms, and data. A strength is how it closes the book by reconnecting early critical theory to digital capitalism. A limit is that mediatization theory, developed mostly in Northern Europe, can overstate media's autonomous logic and flatten differences across regions and communities. It frames Polson's work on geo-social media and place, and prepares for Banet-Weiser, Couldry and Mejias, and Roberts.

title: A gateway to the global city: Mobile place-making practices by expats
apa: Polson, E. (2015). A gateway to the global city: Mobile place-making practices by expats. *New Media & Society, 17*(4), 629-645.
summary: Through ethnographic work with expatriate professionals in Paris, Polson studies how platforms such as meetup groups help mobile workers build a sense of belonging. She argues that participants use digital media to make an international community that can be carried from one city to the next.
analysis: The study uses participant observation and interviews to show how location-based digital organizing turns global cities into navigable places for a mobile professional class. Its contribution is the idea of mobile place-making, which links digital media to a new global middle class, a theme developed in her book Privileged mobilities. Polson recognizes real benefits, especially for women moving alone, while warning that platforms make placelessness a norm of professional labor. A limit is that the focus on relatively privileged, largely Western expats leaves out migrants whose mobility is constrained, although that contrast is part of the argument. It connects to chapter 14 on commodified community, to Couldry and Mejias on platforms extracting social life, and to research on who gets to be mobile in a global media economy.
note: Syllabus lists only Polson. Chose her New Media & Society article (online first 2013, print 2015) as the best article-length fit; alternatives are a chapter of Privileged mobilities (Peter Lang, 2016) or Halegoua and Polson (2021), Exploring digital placemaking, Convergence, 27(2). DOI not verified, so doi_url is null.

title: Empowered: Popular feminism and popular misogyny
apa: Banet-Weiser, S. (2018). *Empowered: Popular feminism and popular misogyny*. Duke University Press.
summary: Banet-Weiser analyzes the rise of popular feminism, visible in advertising, celebrity, and social media, alongside a networked popular misogyny that reacts to it. She argues that feminism now circulates in an economy of visibility where being seen is treated as the goal, and that misogyny grows in the same space.
analysis: The book reads corporate campaigns, confidence and empowerment programs, and online misogynist movements as a linked cultural formation. Its central contribution is the economy of visibility, in which feminist messages succeed to the degree that they are marketable and individualized, while structural critique is muted. It also shows popular misogyny adopting the language of injury and empowerment, a mirror image of popular feminism. A limit is that the analysis centers United States and British media and largely white, middle-class forms of feminism, which Dosekun's transnational work pushes against. It connects to Fredrickson et al. on self-surveillance, Hearn on branding, chapter 14 on commodification, and the manosphere research noted in chapter 6.
note: Syllabus lists only Banet-Weiser. Chose Empowered (2018), likely the introduction or chapter 1; the alternative is Authentic (NYU Press, 2012). Confirm which chapter is assigned.

title: For Western girls only? Post-feminism as transnational culture
apa: Dosekun, S. (2015). For Western girls only? Post-feminism as transnational culture. *Feminist Media Studies, 15*(6), 960-975. https://doi.org/10.1080/14680777.2015.1062991
summary: Dosekun challenges the assumption that postfeminism is a Western phenomenon that non-Western women only receive secondhand. Drawing on research with class-privileged women in Lagos, Nigeria, she argues that postfeminism is a transnationally circulating culture that women elsewhere can take up on their own terms.
analysis: The article combines theoretical critique with qualitative interviews with young, affluent Nigerian women about fashion and femininity. Its contribution is a transnational analytic that refuses both the Western default in postfeminism studies and the idea that non-Western women are merely imitating. It highlights class as the axis that makes postfeminist consumption available across borders. A limit, which Dosekun acknowledges, is that her participants are an elite minority, so the account says more about global class formation than about Nigerian women broadly. It directly corrects the Western frame of Banet-Weiser and chapter 8's body image research, and it echoes Henderson's call to decenter whiteness in media studies.
note: Syllabus lists only Dosekun. Chose this open-access article over Fashioning postfeminism (University of Illinois Press, 2020) because it is the article-length statement of the same argument. read_url is the Sussex repository record, open access since 2017. Some records list issue 4; Sussex and Taylor and Francis list 15(6), 960-975.

title: Data colonialism: Rethinking big data's relation to the contemporary subject
apa: Couldry, N., & Mejias, U. A. (2019). Data colonialism: Rethinking big data's relation to the contemporary subject. *Television & New Media, 20*(4), 336-349. https://doi.org/10.1177/1527476418796632
summary: Couldry and Mejias argue that the continuous extraction of data from everyday life is best understood as a new form of colonialism rather than only a new phase of capitalism. Data relations, they claim, appropriate human life as a resource in the way historical colonialism appropriated land and labor.
analysis: This is a theoretical essay that builds its case by analogy with historical colonialism and by extending Marx's account of how capitalism annexes new domains. Its contribution is to name data extraction as appropriation, which explains why it is treated as natural and free and why it enables discrimination and behavioral manipulation. The framework revives Smythe's audience commodity and chapter 14's commodification for the platform age. Critics, including decolonial scholars, argue that the colonial analogy risks flattening the violence of historical colonialism and centers Northern platforms and theorists, though the authors explicitly include China's platforms. It connects to Roberts on the labor behind platforms, to Smythe, and to research on algorithmic classification.
note: Syllabus lists Couldry and Mejias; chose the Television & New Media article (online 2018) over the book The costs of connection (Stanford University Press, 2019). read_url is the LSE Research Online record with the accepted manuscript.

title: Behind the screen: Content moderation in the shadows of social media
apa: Roberts, S. T. (2019). *Behind the screen: Content moderation in the shadows of social media*. Yale University Press.
summary: Roberts documents the hidden workforce of commercial content moderators who screen violent, abusive, and disturbing material for social media platforms. Based on interviews with moderators in the United States and the Philippines, she shows how this labor is outsourced, low status, psychologically harmful, and deliberately kept out of view.
analysis: The book draws on years of interviews and fieldwork across in-house, contract, and offshore moderation settings. Its central contribution is to make commercial content moderation visible as a core function of platforms, undercutting the image of platforms as neutral conduits. It shows how global outsourcing maps moderation onto older colonial and racialized divisions of labor. A limit is that access constraints mean the evidence comes from a limited set of workers and firms, and the book predates the large-scale shift to automated and AI-assisted moderation. It pairs with Couldry and Mejias on extraction, extends Smythe's labor analysis, and complicates chapter 3's normative debates about platform responsibility.
note: Syllabus lists only Roberts; chose Sarah T. Roberts, Behind the screen. ISBN is the 2019 Yale hardcover; confirm which chapter is assigned.
